_about: Best published collision attacks (standard IV, complete hash) on reduced-round SHA-256, SHA3-256 and BLAKE3, before HashSmash. log2T in each paper's own unit (calls to the reduced hash). 'source' says where the number was read. log2T null: 'practical' marks a real collision without a stated complexity; otherwise the figure is unknown.

attacks.ref: Sanadhya, Sarkar, INDOCRYPT 2008 (ePrint 2008/270), with a 2^32-entry table (memory 2^37: the table)
Mendel, Nad, Schläffer, ASIACRYPT 2011: practical 27-step collision
Mendel, Nad, Schläffer, EUROCRYPT 2013: practical 28-step collision
No 32-step figure published; practical collisions exist for 31 steps (ASIACRYPT 2024) and 35 steps (ePrint 2026/1080)
Li, Liu, Wang, Shi, CRYPTO 2026 (ePrint 2026/1080): practical 35-step collision
Li, Liu, Wang, Shi, CRYPTO 2026 (ePrint 2026/1080), memory 2^53.0
Li, Zhang, Li, Liu, Qian, Zhu (ePrint 2026/1120), negligible memory
Li, Zhang, Li, Liu, Qian, Zhu (ePrint 2026/1120): first 38-step collision attack, negligible memory; 2^100 first blocks x 2^4 dominate
Dinur, Dunkelman, Shamir, FSE 2012: practical 4-round Keccak-256 collision
Guo, Liao, Liu, Liu, Qiao, Song, J. Cryptology 2020 (ePrint 2019/147): real collision; trail weight 36.70, 45.6 h search after a 428.8 h connector
Guo, Liu, Song, Tu, ASIACRYPT 2022 (ePrint 2022/184): classical attacks do not reach 6-round SHA3-256 (quantum only)

noPriorAttack.note: No published collision attack on the hash of BLAKE, BLAKE2 or BLAKE3 at any round count (BLAKE3 spec, Table 4; ePrint and arXiv searches). Published results are preimages (2.5 rounds), compression-function near-collisions (4 rounds) and boomerang distinguishers.
No classical collision attack (ePrint 2022/184); none since, per ePrint 2026/2107.

history._about: Full (not reduced-round) hash functions. Green: no collision attack; red: collisions found in practice. MD5 starts green here (Zooko's survey has it yellow for its 128-bit output).

lanes.name: MD5
collisions: August 2004: Wang, Feng, Lai and Yu announce MD5 collisions at the CRYPTO rump session (ePrint 2004/199). Found in about an hour on an IBM p690; the first collision for a widely used hash.

December 2008: Sotirov, Stevens, Appelbaum, Lenstra, Molnar, Osvik and de Weger present a forged CA certificate at 25C3, built with an MD5 chosen-prefix collision on 200 PlayStation 3s. Trusted by every browser; CRYPTO 2009 paper.
May 2012: the Flame espionage malware is found (Kaspersky, CrySyS, Iran CERT). Its forged Microsoft code-signing certificate used a new MD5 chosen-prefix collision.
other: 1993: den Boer and Bosselaers find a pseudo-collision of MD5's compression function (same message, two different IVs). EUROCRYPT 1993.
1996: Dobbertin finds collisions of MD5's compression function for a chosen IV, and recommends against new uses of MD5. Not a collision of the hash.
ranges: Flame's forged certificate was in use before discovery; Kaspersky's analysis dates the operation to at least 2010, and some analyses suggest 2007.

lanes.name: SHA-1
collisions: February 2005: Wang, Yin and Yu announce a SHA-1 collision attack in 2^69 operations, far below the 2^80 birthday bound (CRYPTO 2005). No collision is produced, but NIST begins planning the move away from SHA-1.
February 2017: Stevens, Bursztein, Karpman, Albertini and Markov (CWI and Google) publish the first SHA-1 collision: two PDFs, about 2^63 computations, 6,500 CPU-years plus 110 GPU-years.
January 2020: Leurent and Peyrin publish 'SHA-1 is a Shambles', the first chosen-prefix SHA-1 collision (about 2^63.4), and use it to impersonate a PGP key. USENIX Security 2020.
other: October 2015: Stevens, Karpman and Peyrin publish 'the SHAppening', a freestart collision of SHA-1's compression function (attacker-chosen IV), about 2^57 on GPUs. EUROCRYPT 2016.

lanes.name: SHA-256
events: August 2002: FIPS 180-2 publishes SHA-256 (drafted 2001). No collision attack on the full 64-step function has been published; the best reach 38 of 64 steps (2026).

lanes.name: Keccak · SHA-3
events: October 2012: NIST selects Keccak (Bertoni, Daemen, Peeters, Van Assche) as the winner of the SHA-3 competition, from 64 entries.
August 2015: NIST publishes FIPS 202, standardising SHA3-224/256/384/512 and SHAKE128/256.

lanes.name: BLAKE family
events: December 2012: Aumasson, Neves, Wilcox-O'Hearn and Winnerlein publish BLAKE2, a faster BLAKE with fewer rounds (10 for BLAKE2s, 12 for BLAKE2b).
January 2020: O'Connor, Aumasson, Neves and Wilcox-O'Hearn publish BLAKE3: 7 rounds, a Merkle tree mode, and parallelism.

history.sources: Colours and design years: Zooko's survey (2017). Events: Wang et al. CRYPTO 2004 rump / ePrint 2004/199 (MD5), Sotirov et al. 25C3 2008 (rogue CA), Wang et al. CRYPTO 2005 (SHA-1 2^69), Stevens et al. 2017 (SHAttered), Leurent and Peyrin, USENIX Security 2020 (chosen prefix); den Boer and Bosselaers EUROCRYPT 1993, Dobbertin 1996, Stevens, Karpman and Peyrin EUROCRYPT 2016 (freestart). Flame: discovered May 2012 (Kaspersky, CrySyS, Iran CERT); its forged Microsoft certificate used an MD5 chosen-prefix collision (Microsoft SRD blog, June 2012; Stevens' analysis). Kaspersky's analysis dated its operation to at least 2010, so the bar runs from 2010 to discovery.

_aliases: Preferred display names, by the solver's request. The Yukon handle stays in parentheses so submissions can be looked up.
_mem: mem: log2 bytes of memory; null = negligible (counted as 0); 'unknown' = not stated where read. Under Zooko's metric cost = log2T + mem.
_metric: Zooko's survey counts an attack as cheaper than brute force only if time × memory is below brute force (Bernstein 2005). Generic collision search (van Oorschot–Wiener) runs in 2^128 with negligible memory, so the generic line stays at 128 under both metrics.

designs._about: Round counts chosen by designers over time, per family. Each entry: [year, rounds, name].
